questions.question: Explain why a main sequence star stays the same size for billions of years.
questions.expected_answer: Gravity pulls the star's gas inwards, while the energy released by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in the core heats the gas, so the hot gas and radiation push outwards. These forces balance (equilibrium). The balance is self-correcting: if the core heats, the star expands and cools, slowing fusion; if it cools, gravity compresses and heats it.

questions.question: Arrange the star colours red, white, blue, yellow and orange from coolest to hottest, and state approximate temperatures for the coolest and hottest.
questions.expected_answer: Red (about 3 000 °C), orange, yellow, white, blue (about 20 000 °C to over 30 000 °C).

questions.question: Explain why massive stars have much shorter lives than the Sun, even though they contain more hydrogen.
questions.expected_answer: A more massive star has stronger gravity, which squeezes its core harder, making it hotter and denser, so fusion happens much faster. The star uses its fuel at a far greater rate than its extra fuel makes up for, so it runs out after only a few million to tens of millions of years, compared with about 10 billion years for the Sun.
